learnings.title: Design a news feed
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The most-asked frontend system design question, and the one with the most ways to sound generic. What separates a strong answer is recognising that "feed" is three independent problems that happen to share a screen. ![News feed — request split, virtualization, cursor pagination](/diagrams/sysdesign/news-feed.svg) ## R — Requirements **Functional** - Scroll an infinite, ranked feed of posts - Each post: author, text, optional media, like/comment counts - Like and unlike, with the count updating immediately - New posts arriving while you read are surfaced, not injected **Non-functional** - First post readable < 1.5 s at p75 on 4G / mid-range Android - Smooth 60 fps scroll on a thousand-post session - Works on a flaky connection; a failed page does not empty the screen - WCAG AA: keyboard reachable, correct list semantics **Scope I'd cut:** composing posts, ranking itself, moderation, notifications. **The question that decides everything:** > "Is the ordering ranked-per-user or chronological? If it's personalised, nothing is cacheable at the edge and this becomes a different design." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD U["Feed route"] --> V["VirtualList"] V --> P["PostCard"] U --> S["IntersectionObserver sentinel"] U --> B["New-posts banner"] U --> D["Data layer
useInfiniteQuery"] D --> E["CDN edge — ranked ids"] D --> O["Origin — /me/overlay"] ``` **Rendering:** streaming SSR for the first screen. The feed is the LCP element, and a personalised feed cannot be static. Stream the shell immediately and let the ranked ids resolve into it. ### Problem 1 — the request is personalised, so nothing caches The naive `GET /feed` returns ranked posts *and* my likes and saves. That is per-user, so no shared cache may hold it, and every reader pays full origin latency. Split it by ownership: | Request | Contents | Cacheability | | --- | --- | --- | | `GET /feed?cursor=` | Ranked post ids + content | `public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` — edge, ~30 ms | | `GET /me/overlay?ids=` | My likes, my saves for those ids | `private, no-store` — origin, ~80 ms, tiny | > "One 250 ms uncacheable request becomes a 30 ms edge hit plus a small personal call that can land *after* first paint. The posts render immediately; the like buttons fill in a moment later." If ranking is per-individual rather than per-cohort, say so and drop the edge cache — but propose cohort bucketing as the thing that would restore it. ### Problem 2 — the list outgrows the DOM A long session accumulates thousands of posts. At ~8 nodes per post, 10,000 posts is 80,000 DOM nodes: over 100 MB of memory, and every style recalculation walks all of it. **Virtualize.** Render the visible window plus overscan, recycle nodes on scroll. The costs, which you should name unprompted: - **Variable heights.** Posts with and without media differ. Measure and cache per item, and use an estimate before measurement. - **Scroll restoration** becomes yours to implement — save the anchor item id and offset, not `scrollTop`. - **Ctrl+F stops working** for anything off screen. A real UX regression; worth stating you accepted it. - **Accessibility.** With 30 nodes in the DOM, a screen reader announces "30 items". Set `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` on each row, or the list lies. ### Problem 3 — the list mutates while you read it Offset pagination on a live feed is a **correctness bug**: a post inserted between page 1 and page 2 shifts everything, so page 2 repeats an item and silently drops another. ```javascript GET /feed?cursor=eyJpZCI6UDd9&limit=20 → { items: [...], nextCursor: 'eyJpZCI6UDR9' | null } ``` Cursor pagination is stable under insertion. New posts do not get injected into the scroll position — they go to a **"12 new posts" banner** at the top, because inserting content above the reader's viewport is a layout shift and a CLS penalty. ## D — Data model Normalised, because a post appears in the feed, in search, and on its own page, and liking it once must update all three. ```javascript { posts: { p1: { id, authorId, body, mediaId, likeCount, commentCount } }, users: { u9: { id, name, avatarUrl } }, media: { m4: { id, url, width, height } }, // width/height reserve space feed: { pages: [{ ids: [...], cursor }], status: 'ready' }, viewer: { likedPostIds: Set, savedPostIds: Set }, // from the overlay call } ``` `media.width` and `media.height` are load-bearing: without them every image that loads shifts the layout, and CLS is a vitals failure. ## I — Interface ```javascript // Network GET /feed?cursor=&limit=20 → { items, nextCursor } GET /me/overlay?ids=p1,p2,… → { liked: [...], saved: [...] } POST /posts/:id/like → { likeCount } // Idempotency-Key required // Component heights.get(i) ?? 320} onEndReached={fetchNextPage} renderItem={(post) => } state="loading" | "ready" | "error" | "end" /> ``` ## O — Optimisations ### Optimistic likes ```javascript const like = useMutation({ mutationFn: (id) => api.like(id, { idempotencyKey: keyFor(id) }), onMutate: async (id) => { await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['post', id] }); const prev = qc.getQueryData(['post', id]); qc.setQueryData(['post', id], (p) => ({ ...p, likeCount: p.likeCount + 1 })); return { prev }; // snapshot for rollback }, onError: (_e, id, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(['post', id], ctx.prev), onSettled: (_d, _e, id) => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['post', id] }), }); ``` Because the cache is normalised, one entity update corrects every list showing that post. ### Images The single biggest payload, and the usual LCP element: - `srcset` + `sizes` so a phone never downloads a desktop image - AVIF with a WebP fallback - `loading="lazy"` below the fold, `fetchpriority="high"` on the first image - **Always** `width` and `height`, or an `aspect-ratio` box — this is the CLS fix - A blurhash or dominant-colour placeholder so the space is never blank ### Scroll performance - `content-visibility: auto` on off-screen cards lets the browser skip their layout entirely - Never touch layout properties in a scroll handler; `IntersectionObserver` for the sentinel - Passive listeners; no synchronous `getBoundingClientRect` in the scroll path ### Failure and empty states Four states, all designed: **loading** (skeletons at the right heights, so no shift), **empty** (a first-run feed with nothing in it), **error** (a retry that keeps the posts already loaded on screen), **end** (you have reached the bottom — the one everyone forgets). ### Accessibility `
    `/`
  • ` semantics with `aria-setsize`/`aria-posinset`; the new-posts banner as an `aria-live="polite"` region; focus never lost when a page appends; like buttons with `aria-pressed`. ## Common mistakes - **Offset pagination.** Duplicates and drops; it is wrong, not just suboptimal. - **Injecting new posts inline.** Layout shift and lost reading position. - **No image dimensions.** Guaranteed CLS failure. - **Virtualizing without fixing the a11y tree.** The list now lies about its size. - **Treating "personalised" as unavoidable.** Splitting the response is the whole trick. - **Forgetting the end-of-feed state.** An infinite spinner at the bottom of a finite list. ## Key takeaways - Three independent problems: an uncacheable request, a DOM that outgrows the device, and a list that mutates under the reader. - Split the response so the bulk of it caches at the edge and only a tiny personal overlay hits the origin. - Virtualize, and name the costs: variable heights, scroll restoration, Ctrl+F, and the accessibility tree. - Cursor pagination is correctness; new posts go to a banner, never inline. - Normalised cache so one optimistic like corrects every view of that post. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Ranking is per-individual, not per-cohort."** — The edge cache is gone. Propose cohort bucketing, or cache only the post bodies by id and fetch the ranked id list uncached. - **"A user scrolls for twenty minutes."** — Memory. Virtualization caps the DOM; also drop pages far above the viewport from the cache and refetch on scroll back. - **"How do you keep counts fresh?"** — They do not need to be exact. Poll or SSE for visible posts only, and reconcile on scroll into view. - **"Video autoplay in the feed?"** — `IntersectionObserver` at a threshold, one playing at a time, muted, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion` and `saveData`.

learnings.title: Design a chat / messaging app
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Chat looks simple and is not. Every hard part is invisible on a good connection: ordering, identity, the reconnect gap, and what a message's state means to the person who sent it.

![Chat — message lifecycle, ordering and the reconnect gap](/diagrams/sysdesign/chat.svg)

## R — Requirements

**Functional**
- 1:1 and group conversations; send and receive text
- Message states visible to the sender: sending, sent, delivered, read
- Typing indicators and presence
- History on scroll-back
- Unread counts per conversation

**Non-functional**
- A sent message appears **instantly** — no waiting on the network
- Messages never silently disappear, in any failure mode
- Order is identical on every device
- Survives a disconnect and resumes without loss
- 10,000-message conversations scroll smoothly

**The scoping question:**

> "How many people in a conversation? 1:1 and a 10-person group are the same design. A 10,000-person channel is not — at that point you cannot fan out to every client and presence alone becomes the hard problem."

## A — Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  UI["Conversation view"] --> L["Local store (IndexedDB)"]
  UI --> OB["Outbox"]
  OB --> S["Sync engine"]
  S <-->|WebSocket| G["Gateway"]
  S -->|"REST on reconnect"| H["GET /messages?after=seq"]
  G --> S
  S --> L
  L --> UI
```

**The shape that matters:** the UI reads and writes the **local store**, never the network. A separate sync engine reconciles. If your send handler awaits a fetch, you do not have a chat app — you have a form with a slow submit.

**Transport: WebSocket**, and this is one of the few designs that genuinely needs it — typing indicators, read receipts and acks are all client→server.

## D — Data model

```javascript
{
  conversations: {
    c1: { id, participantIds, lastMessageSeq, unreadCount, lastReadSeq },
  },
  messages: {
    // Keyed by CLIENT id, because it exists before the server one does.
    'tmp-8f3a': {
      clientId: 'tmp-8f3a',   // also the idempotency key
      serverId: null,
      seq: null,              // server-assigned; THIS is the sort key
      conversationId: 'c1',
      body: 'hey',
      sentAt: 1736…,          // client clock — display only, never ordering
      status: 'sending',      // sending | sent | delivered | read | failed
    },
  },
  byConversation: { c1: ['tmp-8f3a', 'm-1041', …] },
  outbox: ['tmp-8f3a'],
  connection: 'online' | 'reconnecting' | 'offline',
}
```

### Two ids, and why

The client must render the message before the server has heard of it, so the client mints an id. When the ack arrives, **reconcile by client id, not by list position** — the list has moved.

That same client id is the **idempotency key**. A retry after a dropped response cannot create a duplicate, which is the single most common chat bug.

### Order by server sequence, never by timestamp

Client clocks are wrong — by seconds, sometimes by hours, and sometimes deliberately. Two users' messages interleaved by client timestamp produce different orders on different devices. The server assigns a monotonic `seq` per conversation and **that** is the sort key. `sentAt` is for display only.

## I — Interface

```javascript
// WebSocket, both directions
→ { type: 'message.send', clientId, conversationId, body }
← { type: 'message.ack', clientId, serverId, seq }
← { type: 'message.new', message }
← { type: 'typing', conversationId, userId }
→ { type: 'read', conversationId, upToSeq }

// REST for anything a socket is bad at
GET /conversations/:id/messages?before=seq&limit=50   // scroll-back
GET /conversations/:id/messages?after=seq             // the reconnect gap
```

## O — Optimisations

### The reconnect gap — the highest-value follow-up

A socket drops for two minutes. Messages 1042–1045 arrive during the gap. On reconnect, a naive client subscribes to new messages and **never learns those four existed**. Nothing errors. The conversation is simply wrong.

```javascript
async function onReconnect() {
  const lastSeq = await local.getLastSeq(conversationId);
  // 1 · Backfill the gap before trusting the live stream.
  const missed = await api.messages({ after: lastSeq });
  await local.merge(missed);
  // 2 · Only now replay our own unsent messages. The client ids
  //     are the idempotency keys, so anything the server already
  //     got is a no-op rather than a duplicate.
  for (const clientId of await outbox.all()) resend(clientId);
}
```

Backoff with **jitter** on reconnect — without it, every client in the region reconnects at the same instant and re-kills a recovering gateway.

### Optimistic send, honestly rendered

```javascript
async function send(body) {
  const clientId = crypto.randomUUID();
  await local.messages.put({ clientId, body, status: 'sending', seq: null });
  await outbox.add(clientId);          // durable — survives a reload
  socket.send({ type: 'message.send', clientId, body });
}
```

Sort messages with `seq ?? Infinity` so pending ones sit at the bottom until acknowledged, then slot into place. Render `sending` in a subdued style — **a failure that looks identical to a success is the bug users report as "it never sent".**

### Scroll-back and virtualization

Chat scrolls *upward*, which makes it harder than a feed:

- **Anchor the scroll position** when prepending older messages, or the view jumps. Save the top visible message id and its offset, prepend, then restore.
- Keep the view pinned to the bottom **only if the user was already at the bottom** — never yank someone reading history down to a new message.
- Virtualize with variable heights (images, replies, reactions all differ).

### Typing indicators

Throttle to roughly one event every 2–3 seconds while typing, and expire client-side after ~5 seconds of silence. Never send one per keystroke — that is a keystroke logger's traffic profile and it will melt your gateway.

### Accessibility

The message list is an `aria-live="polite"` **log** region (`role="log"`), so a screen reader announces new messages without stealing focus. Each message needs its sender and time in its accessible name; status is text, not a colour alone.

## Common mistakes

- **Resuming from "now".** Silent message loss — the worst possible chat failure.
- **Ordering by client timestamp.** Different devices show different orders.
- **No idempotency key.** Duplicates on every retry.
- **Reconciling by position.** The list moved between send and ack.
- **Awaiting the network in the send handler.** Every message feels slow.
- **An in-memory outbox.** A reload loses unsent messages.
- **Typing events per keystroke.** Gateway load for no benefit.

## Key takeaways

- The UI talks to a local store; a sync engine talks to the network.
- Two ids — client id for identity and idempotency, server seq for ordering.
- Order by server sequence; client clocks cannot be trusted.
- Reconnect means backfill from your last seq, *then* replay the outbox.
- Message state must be visible, and failure must not look like success.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Two devices, same account."** — Both need the full event stream and a per-device read cursor. Read state is per user; delivery state is per device.
- **"Messages sent while fully offline?"** — The outbox is in IndexedDB, so it survives a reload. Flush on reconnect and on app start, not just on the `online` event.
- **"A 10,000-person channel?"** — Stop fanning out to every client. Only subscribe to the visible conversation, sample presence rather than tracking everyone, and paginate the member list.
- **"How do you show 'read' without leaking?"** — It is a product decision with privacy weight. Say that, then implement it as a per-conversation `upToSeq` cursor.

learnings.title: Design an autocomplete / typeahead search
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
A deceptively small component that tests three things at once: network discipline, a genuinely difficult accessibility pattern, and whether you have ever debugged a race condition. ![Autocomplete — the out-of-order response race](/diagrams/sysdesign/autocomplete.svg) ## R — Requirements **Functional** - Suggestions appear as the user types, from ~2 characters - Full keyboard control: arrows, Enter, Escape, Tab - Selecting navigates or fills the input - Recent searches when the input is empty **Non-functional** - Suggestions within 100 ms of a pause — this is the one thing that must feel instant - Never show results for a query the user has moved past - Fully usable with a screen reader - Must not fire a request per keystroke **The scoping question:** > "How big is the corpus? A few hundred items I'd ship to the client and filter locally — zero latency, no backend. Millions and it's a server round trip per query, which is a completely different design." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR I["Input"] --> D["Debounce 150ms"] D --> C["Cache hit?"] C -->|yes| R["Render"] C -->|no| Q["Abort previous
fetch with seq"] Q --> G["Seq guard"] G -->|current| R G -->|stale| X["Discard"] ``` ### The race — the whole point of the question Type `r`, `re`, `rea`, `reac`. Four requests. The network does not promise you they return in order — and the response for `re` arriving last will overwrite the results for `reac`. **The input says one thing and the list shows another.** This never reproduces on a fast connection, which is exactly why it ships. Three defences, and you need all three: ```javascript function useSuggestions(query) { const [results, setResults] = useState([]); const seq = useRef(0); const controller = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { if (query.length < 2) { setResults([]); return; } // 1 · Debounce — a fast typist sends one request, not six. const timer = setTimeout(async () => { // 2 · Abort the previous request so it cannot resolve. controller.current?.abort(); controller.current = new AbortController(); const mine = ++seq.current; try { const res = await fetch(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal: controller.current.signal, }); const data = await res.json(); // 3 · Refuse anything older than the newest response rendered. // Abort alone is not enough: a response already in flight // can still land. if (mine === seq.current) setResults(data.items); } catch (err) { if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setResults([]); } }, 150); return () => clearTimeout(timer); }, [query]); return results; } ``` **Why all three:** debounce reduces volume but does not order anything. Abort helps but a response mid-flight can still arrive. Only the sequence guard actually guarantees you never render a stale result. ### Debounce or throttle? **Debounce**, and the distinction is worth saying out loud: throttle fires at a steady rate during typing, which sends requests for prefixes nobody wanted. Debounce waits for a pause, which is exactly when the user wants an answer. 150 ms is the usual sweet spot — long enough to skip intermediate keystrokes, short enough to feel immediate. ## D — Data model ```javascript { query: 'reac', // controlled input cache: Map, // per query string results: Suggestion[], // what is rendered now activeIndex: -1, // keyboard highlight, -1 = none status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'ready' | 'empty' | 'error', recent: string[], // shown when query is empty } ``` `activeIndex` is deliberately separate from focus: **focus stays in the input** the whole time. That is what makes the accessibility pattern work. ## I — Interface ```javascript GET /search/suggest?q=reac&limit=8 → { items: [{ id, text, type, highlight: [[0,4]] }] } void} getSuggestions={fn} minChars={2} debounceMs={150} emptyMessage="No matches" /> ``` The server returning `highlight` ranges rather than HTML matters: **never** `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` on a search response. Ranges let the client wrap matched substrings in `` safely. ## O — Optimisations ### Caching and prefetch ```javascript // Exact-query cache makes backspace instant — the previous query // is already in the map. if (cache.has(query)) return cache.get(query); ``` Cache per query string, keep a bounded LRU (~50 entries). Optionally prefetch on focus so the first keystroke already has recent searches on screen. ### Accessibility — the combobox pattern This is where most candidates lose the question. The ARIA pattern is specific and unforgiving: ```html aria-autocomplete="list" />
  • react
8 suggestions available
``` The rules that matter: - **Focus never leaves the input.** Arrow keys move `aria-activedescendant`, not DOM focus. Moving real focus into the list breaks typing. - **Announce the result count** in a polite live region, or a screen reader user has no idea anything appeared. - **Escape** closes the list and keeps the typed text; a second Escape clears it. - **Arrow down from the last item** wraps to the first (or stops — pick one and be consistent). - **Touch targets ≥ 44 px**, and the list must not be hidden by the on-screen keyboard. ### Failure and edge cases | Case | Behaviour | | --- | --- | | No results | "No matches for *reac*" — never an empty box | | Request fails | Keep the input usable; fail silently or offer retry. Never block typing | | Slow response | Spinner only after ~300 ms, so fast responses never flash it | | Fast typist | Debounce plus abort means one request | | Paste | Fires immediately; do not wait for the debounce on a paste event | | IME composition | Do not search mid-composition — listen for `compositionend` | That last one matters for Japanese, Chinese and Korean input and is an easy differentiator to mention. ### When to skip the network entirely > "Under a few thousand items I'd ship the corpus to the client, build a trie or use a small fuzzy matcher, and filter locally. Zero latency, works offline, and the race condition cannot exist. It only becomes a server problem when the corpus is too big to ship." ## Common mistakes - **No cancellation or sequence guard.** The signature bug of this question. - **Throttle instead of debounce.** Requests for prefixes nobody wanted. - **Moving focus into the list.** Breaks typing and breaks screen readers. - **No live region.** Screen reader users are never told anything appeared. - **Rendering server HTML for highlighting.** An XSS vector in a search box. - **A spinner on every keystroke.** Visual noise on fast connections. ## Key takeaways - Debounce, abort, and a sequence guard — all three, because each covers a gap the others leave. - The race never reproduces on fast networks, which is why it reaches production. - Focus stays in the input; `aria-activedescendant` moves the highlight. - Announce result counts in a live region and design the empty state. - Small corpus means no network at all — say so before designing a backend. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do you handle a really slow response?"** — Delay the spinner ~300 ms, keep the previous results visible rather than blanking, and never block typing. - **"Search across three entity types?"** — Grouped `role="group"` sections inside one listbox, one flat keyboard sequence across groups, and headers that are not themselves selectable. - **"How would you test the race?"** — Mock fetch with controllable resolution order, resolve them out of order, and assert the stale response is discarded.

learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum

YouTube/Netflix-style. The interviewer is not asking you to write a decoder — they want to know whether you understand **adaptive bitrate**, and that a stall hurts a viewer far more than a lower resolution they will probably not notice. ![Adaptive bitrate — the quality-selection loop](/diagrams/sysdesign/video-player.svg) ## R — Requirements **Functional:** play/pause, seek, volume, fullscreen; automatic quality with a manual override; captions; resume where you left off; a preview thumbnail on the scrub bar. **Non-functional:** playback starts in under ~2 s; no rebuffering on a variable connection; works on mobile and desktop; captions and keyboard control are non-negotiable. > "Live or on-demand? Live has a latency target and a sliding window instead of a fixed duration — the buffering strategy inverts, because you cannot buffer ahead of content that does not exist yet." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD M["Manifest (.m3u8 / .mpd)"] --> A["ABR controller"] BW["Bandwidth estimate"] --> A BUF["Buffer level"] --> A A --> F["Fetch next segment"] F --> MSE["MediaSource
SourceBuffer"] MSE --> V["<video>"] V --> BUF ``` ### The pieces **HLS or DASH**, both the same idea: the content is cut into 2–6 second segments and encoded at several bitrates. learnings.title: Design a collaborative document editor
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The hardest common frontend design question, and the one where the correct answer includes "I would not build this part myself". ![Last-write-wins vs OT vs CRDT](/diagrams/sysdesign/collab-editor.svg) ## R — Requirements **Functional** - Multiple people edit one document simultaneously - Remote cursors and selections are visible - Changes appear within ~100 ms - Undo/redo that undoes *your* edits, not everyone's - Offline editing that syncs on reconnect **Non-functional** - **No edit is ever silently lost** — the requirement that drives the whole design - All replicas converge to the same document - Typing stays responsive at any document size - Works with a screen reader **The scoping question that changes everything:** > "Plain text, rich text, or structured blocks? Plain text is a solved problem with a library. Rich text means formatting marks that also have to merge — bold applied across a range someone else is editing — and that is an order of magnitude more work." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR E["Editor view
(ProseMirror / Lexical)"] --> D["CRDT document
(Yjs)"] D --> P["Provider
(y-websocket)"] P <--> S["Sync server"] S --> Per["Persistence
+ compaction"] D --> A["Awareness
cursors, presence"] A --> P ``` Three separable layers, and keeping them separate is the design: 1. **The editor** owns the DOM, input handling, and selection. 2. **The CRDT document** owns the text and its merge semantics. 3. **The provider** owns the network — connection, resync, awareness. ## The core problem Both users hold `"cat"`. A types `s` at position 3. B types `!` at position 3. At the same moment. **Last-write-wins destroys one edit.** Sending the whole document means the second write overwrites the first. Silent data loss — unacceptable, and the reason this question exists. ### OT — Operational Transformation Send *intents* (`insert("s", 3)`), and transform each incoming op against the concurrent ops it did not know about. B's insert at 3 becomes an insert at 4 because A already put a character there. - **Needs a central server** to pick the canonical order - Small payloads, simple ops - **Famously hard to get right.** The transform function must be correct for every pair of operation types, and a subtle bug corrupts documents in ways users cannot recover from ### CRDT — Conflict-free Replicated Data Type Give every character a unique, globally orderable id. Both users insert "after `t`"; the tie is broken by comparing ids, deterministically and identically on every replica. **The conflict cannot exist**, so there is nothing to transform. - **No central authority required** — works peer-to-peer and offline - Costs metadata per character; a mature library keeps this manageable through compaction - Deletions leave tombstones, which is why compaction matters ### The answer that scores > "I'd use Yjs. Not because CRDTs are theoretically nicer, but because both OT and CRDT are extremely easy to get subtly wrong, and the failure mode is silently corrupting someone's document. I'd only reach for OT if I had to interoperate with an existing OT server." Naming the *library* and saying why you would not hand-roll it is a senior answer, not a cop-out. Hand-rolling here is how teams lose a quarter. ## D — Data model ```javascript const ydoc = new Y.Doc(); const ytext = ydoc.getText('body'); // CRDT-backed, merges by construction const awareness = provider.awareness; // ephemeral, NOT part of the document awareness.setLocalState({ user: { id, name, colour }, cursor: { anchor, head }, }); ``` The split that matters: **the document is persistent and merged; awareness is ephemeral and lossy.** Cursor positions must never enter the document — they are per-connection, they vanish when you disconnect, and merging them would be meaningless. ## I — Interface ```javascript // The provider handles the wire format; you almost never touch it. const provider = new WebsocketProvider('wss://…', docId, ydoc); // Bind to the editor once; edits flow both ways automatically. new Collaboration({ document: ydoc }); new CollaborationCursor({ provider, user: { name, colour } }); // REST, for what sockets are bad at GET /docs/:id/snapshot // a compacted starting state for a new joiner GET /docs/:id/history // named versions POST /docs/:id/permissions ``` ## O — Optimisations ### What the library does not give you Every one of these is a likely follow-up, and this list is where you show depth: | Concern | The design | | --- | --- | | **Remote cursors** | Awareness protocol; map CRDT positions to DOM ranges. Throttle to ~50 ms — a cursor update per mousemove is a flood | | **Undo** | Scoped to your own origin (`Y.UndoManager` with a tracked origin), or Ctrl+Z undoes a colleague's paragraph | | **Large documents** | Load a compacted snapshot, not the full op log. Compact server-side on a schedule | | **New joiner** | Snapshot + ops since; never replay two years of history | | **Permissions** | Enforced server-side. A read-only client that can still emit ops is not read-only | | **Version history** | Periodic named snapshots — the op log is not a user-facing history | | **Offline** | Persist the doc to IndexedDB (`y-indexeddb`); it merges on reconnect with no extra code | ### Typing performance - The CRDT update is cheap; **rendering** is the cost. Batch remote updates into `requestAnimationFrame`. - Do not re-render the whole document on each keystroke — editor frameworks diff at the node level; keep it that way. - Very large documents: virtualize the rendered viewport, but keep the whole CRDT in memory — you cannot partially load a CRDT and still merge correctly. ### Accessibility The genuinely hard part, and worth flagging honestly: - Remote edits move the document under a screen reader user with no warning - Announce collaborator activity in a **polite** live region, throttled and summarised ("Ada is editing above") — never announce every keystroke - Never move the local user's selection because of a remote edit - Provide a mode that pauses live updates; for some users that is the only way to work > "I'd be honest that live collaborative editing is hard to make pleasant with a screen reader, and I'd ship a 'pause live updates' control rather than pretend the problem is solved." ## Common mistakes - **Hand-rolling OT or a CRDT.** A quarter of work and a document-corruption bug. - **Sending the whole document.** Last-write-wins, silent data loss. - **Cursors inside the document.** They are ephemeral; merging them is meaningless. - **Global undo.** Undoing a colleague's work is a genuinely upsetting bug. - **Replaying the full op log for new joiners.** Slow, and gets slower forever. - **Permissions enforced only in the UI.** The socket is the real API. ## Key takeaways - The requirement is that no edit is ever silently lost; that rules out last-write-wins immediately. - OT transforms intents and needs a central ordering authority; CRDTs make the conflict impossible and need none. - Use Yjs or Automerge — naming the library and refusing to hand-roll is the strong answer. - Document state and awareness state are separate, and cursors belong to awareness. - Undo must be scoped to your own edits; snapshots, not op logs, serve new joiners. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How does someone joining an hour late catch up?"** — Compacted snapshot plus ops since, not the full log. Compaction is a scheduled server job. - **"Two people bold overlapping ranges?"** — Rich-text marks need their own merge semantics; this is exactly why rich text is much harder than plain text. - **"How do you enforce read-only?"** — Server-side, on the socket. Anything else is a suggestion. - **"The document is 50 MB."** — Virtualize rendering, compact aggressively, and question whether it should be one document at all.

learnings.title: Design a collaborative whiteboard
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Figma/Miro-style. Where the document editor tests merge semantics, the whiteboard tests **rendering** — because the DOM is the wrong tool and saying so is most of the answer. ## R — Requirements **Functional:** draw shapes, freehand, text; select, move, resize, group; infinite pan and zoom; multiple cursors; undo/redo. **Non-functional:** 60 fps while dragging with 10,000 objects on the board; remote edits within ~100 ms; no lost work. > "How many objects on a board, realistically? A hundred and I could do this in SVG. Ten thousand and the DOM is out — that's a canvas or WebGL design." ## A — Architecture ### Why not the DOM 10,000 SVG nodes means 10,000 elements the browser lays out, styles and paints. Dragging one re-runs that. It falls over well before 10,000. | Approach | Ceiling | Trade | | --- | --- | --- | | **SVG / DOM** | ~1,000 objects | Free hit-testing, accessible, CSS-styleable | | **Canvas 2D** | ~10,000 | You implement hit-testing, selection, text rendering | | **WebGL** | 100,000+ | Everything above, plus shaders and no text at all for free | > "Canvas 2D for the board. I'd keep the *chrome* — toolbars, context menus, the text editing overlay — in the DOM, because that's where accessibility and text input actually work." ### Layered canvases ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Static layer — everything not moving
redrawn rarely"] --> C["Composite"] A["Active layer — the object being dragged
redrawn every frame"] --> C O["Overlay layer — cursors, selection handles
redrawn every frame, cheap"] --> C D["DOM chrome — toolbar, text input, menus"] --> C ``` The whole performance strategy: **dragging one shape must not redraw 10,000 others.** Lift it to the active layer, redraw only that layer per frame, and composite the untouched static layer back down on drop. ### Spatial indexing Hit-testing 10,000 objects on every mousemove is 10,000 comparisons per event. A quadtree or R-tree turns that into roughly `log n`. The same index answers "what is in the viewport?", which is what makes infinite canvas viable — you only ever draw what is visible. ## D — Data model ```javascript { // CRDT map, so concurrent edits to different shapes just merge. shapes: Y.Map, viewport: { x, y, zoom }, // local only, never shared selection: Set, // local only awareness: { cursor, selection, user }, // ephemeral } ``` **Z-order uses a fractional index**, not an integer. Inserting between `1.0` and `2.0` gives `1.5` — one field changes. With integers, inserting in the middle rewrites every object above it, which merges catastrophically when two people do it at once. Shapes are a CRDT **map keyed by id**, not a list. Two people moving two different shapes touch different keys and merge with no conflict at all. ## O — Optimisations ### The render loop ```javascript // Coalesce every input and remote update into one frame. let dirty = false; function invalidate() { if (dirty) return; dirty = true; requestAnimationFrame(() => { render(); dirty = false; }); } function render() { const visible = index.search(viewportBounds()); // spatial query ctx.setTransform(zoom, 0, 0, zoom, -camera.x * zoom, -camera.y * zoom); ctx.clearRect(...); for (const shape of visible) draw(ctx, shape); // only what is on screen } ``` Two ideas do all the work: **draw only what is visible**, and **draw at most once per frame** regardless of how many events arrived. ### Freehand strokes The pathological case — a pen stroke generates hundreds of points per second. - **Simplify** with Ramer–Douglas–Peucker on stroke end; store ~20 points, not 400 - **Stream coarsely** — broadcast every ~50 ms, not every point. Others see a slightly smoothed line, which nobody notices - Use `getCoalescedEvents()` so the local stroke is still smooth even though you throttle what you send ### Remote cursors Throttle to ~50 ms and **interpolate between updates** rather than teleporting. A cursor that jumps reads as lag; the same data interpolated reads as smooth. ### Accessibility — be honest A canvas is an opaque rectangle to a screen reader. The credible answer is a **parallel accessible representation**: a visually-hidden DOM list of objects with names and positions, keyboard selection that drives the same commands as the mouse, and full keyboard operation for create/move/resize. Claiming a canvas whiteboard is fully accessible is not believable; designing the parallel tree is. ## Common mistakes - **SVG at scale.** Works in the demo, dies at 5,000 objects. - **One canvas, full redraw per frame.** Dragging one shape repaints everything. - **No spatial index.** Hit-testing and viewport culling are both O(n) per event. - **Integer z-order.** Reordering rewrites everything and merges badly. - **Streaming every pointer event.** Floods the socket for invisible precision. - **Ignoring accessibility entirely** rather than designing the parallel tree. ## Key takeaways - Canvas for the board, DOM for the chrome — text input and a11y only work in the DOM. - Layer static/active/overlay so dragging one object never redraws the rest. - A spatial index makes both hit-testing and viewport culling cheap. - CRDT map keyed by shape id, with fractional z-indices. - Simplify and throttle strokes; interpolate remote cursors. ## Interview follow-ups - **"A board with 100,000 objects?"** — WebGL, instanced rendering, and tile-based caching of the static layer at several zoom levels. - **"Two people resize the same shape?"** — Per-property last-write-wins on that shape's map entry. It is visually jarring but never corrupting — and that is the right trade here. - **"How do you export to PNG?"** — Render to an offscreen canvas at the target resolution, ignoring the viewport, in a worker so the UI does not freeze.

learnings.title: Design an analytics dashboard with live charts
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The question that most rewards recognising that **independent widgets** is a data-fetching decision, not a layout one — and then that arriving independently is six chances to reflow the page. ![Dashboard — independent widget queries](/diagrams/sysdesign/analytics-dashboard.svg) ## R — Requirements **Functional:** a grid of widgets (KPI tiles, time series, tables, funnels); a global date range and filters; drill-down; auto-refresh; export; optionally user-configurable layouts. **Non-functional:** something useful on screen in under 1 s even though one query takes seconds; 60 fps interaction on charts with tens of thousands of points; one failing widget does not break the page. > "How fresh does the data need to be? 'Every second' is a streaming design. 'When I open it' is a caching design. Those are very different builds and people say 'real-time' meaning both." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD F["Filter bar — date range, segment
(state lives in the URL)"] --> W1["Widget: Active users"] F --> W2["Widget: Revenue"] F --> W3["Widget: Cohort retention"] W1 --> Q1["useQuery(['w1', filters])"] W2 --> Q2["useQuery(['w2', filters])"] W3 --> Q3["useQuery(['w3', filters])"] ``` ### One query per widget The naive design is `GET /dashboard` returning everything. It is blocked on the slowest query — so the reader waits 2.4 seconds to see a number that was ready in 180 ms. Each widget owns: - **its own query**, keyed by widget id plus the current filters - **its own skeleton**, sized to the real content - **its own error boundary**, so a failure shows a retry in that card and nowhere else > "The retention table takes two and a half seconds because it's a heavy aggregation. There's no reason the active-users tile should wait for it — it's ready in under 200 milliseconds." ### Reserve the space The half people miss: six widgets arriving at six different times is **six layout shifts** unless every card has a fixed-height skeleton. Independent loading without reserved space trades one long wait for a page that jumps around for two seconds — which measures worse and feels worse. ### Filters belong in the URL ```javascript // ?from=2026-08-01&to=2026-08-31&segment=enterprise const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams(); ``` Dashboards exist to be shared. "Look at this spike" is a link, and that only works if the filter state is in the address bar. This is the single most concrete argument for URL state in the whole curriculum. ## D — Data model ```javascript { filters: { from, to, segment, compareTo }, // mirrored from the URL layout: [{ id: 'w1', x, y, w, h, type: 'line', query: 'active_users' }], // React Query owns the data, keyed by widget + filters. // Nothing here duplicates it. } ``` Keeping widget *data* out of your own store and letting the query cache own it is what gives you dedup, background refresh and per-widget loading states for free. ## O — Optimisations ### Chart rendering — pick by point count | Points | Renderer | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | < 1,000 | **SVG** (Recharts, Visx) | Accessible, inspectable, CSS-styleable, easy tooltips | | 1,000–100,000 | **Canvas** | SVG node count becomes the bottleneck | | > 100,000 | **Downsample first**, then canvas | Rendering points smaller than a pixel is wasted work | **Downsampling is usually the real answer.** A 1,200-pixel-wide chart cannot show 100,000 points — there are only 1,200 columns. Use LTTB (Largest-Triangle-Three-Buckets), which preserves the visual shape including spikes, rather than naive every-nth sampling which can delete the spike entirely. Best of all: **downsample server-side**, so you never ship 100,000 points to render 1,200. ### Refresh - Refresh **only visible widgets** — an `IntersectionObserver` per card - Pause when the tab is hidden (`refetchIntervalInBackground: false`) - Stagger intervals so six widgets do not all fire at the same instant - On a filter change, cancel in-flight queries for the old filters ### Export CSV of a large table must not freeze the tab. Generate in a Web Worker and stream; for very large exports, ask the server for a file and email a link. A frozen tab during export is a common and avoidable bug. ### Accessibility — charts are the hard part A chart is meaningless to a screen reader without help: - Every chart has a **text alternative** that states the trend, not the pixels: "Active users, 1 August to 31 August: rose from 4,200 to 7,900, with a dip on 14 August." - Provide a **table view toggle** for every chart. This is the single most effective accessibility feature a dashboard can ship, and sighted users use it too. - Never encode a series by colour alone — use dash patterns or direct labels - Tooltips must be reachable by keyboard, or their information must exist elsewhere - Check contrast on series colours, including against the gridlines ### Configurable layouts If users can arrange widgets: persist the layout per user, use fractional ordering for position (the same reasoning as a Kanban board), and provide keyboard-accessible move and resize — a drag-only grid is not operable for everyone. ## Common mistakes - **One request for the whole dashboard.** Everything waits for the slowest query. - **Independent loading with no reserved space.** Six layout shifts. - **Filters in component state.** Nobody can share a view — the core use case. - **Rendering 100,000 points into 1,200 pixels.** - **Naive every-nth downsampling.** Deletes the spike that was the point. - **Refreshing hidden widgets and background tabs.** - **Charts with no text alternative or table view.** ## Key takeaways - One query per widget, each with its own skeleton and error boundary. - Reserve the space — independent arrival is independent layout shift without it. - Filters in the URL; a dashboard's purpose is to be shared. - SVG under a thousand points, canvas above, downsample with LTTB — ideally server-side. - Every chart needs a text summary and a table view. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Make it real-time."** — Ask what that means. If it is seconds, SSE with coalesced updates per frame. If it is "fresh when I look", a polling interval on visible widgets is simpler and cheaper. - **"50 widgets on one dashboard?"** — Virtualize the grid and only query what is visible. Also push back: 50 widgets is usually a design problem. - **"The same query on five widgets?"** — A shared query key dedupes it automatically; that is exactly what a query cache buys you.

learnings.title: Design an email client
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Gmail-style. The question that most rewards an offline-first answer, because a mailbox is a large, slow-changing dataset that the user wants instantly and repeatedly. ## R — Requirements **Functional:** threaded message list; read, reply, forward; compose with drafts; labels and folders; search; mark read/unread, archive, delete; multi-select bulk actions. **Non-functional:** the list opens instantly on return; 50,000 messages scroll smoothly; works offline for reading and composing; a sent message is never lost. > "How big is a mailbox? A few hundred messages I'd just fetch. Fifty thousand changes everything — that's a local index and a sync protocol, not a list endpoint." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD UI["Thread list + reader"] --> L["IndexedDB
messages, threads, labels"] UI --> O["Outbox — drafts and sends"] L --> S["Sync engine"] O --> S S -->|"delta since historyId"| API["Server"] API --> S ``` **The local store is the source of truth for reading.** The UI never awaits the network to render a list. That is what makes it feel like a native client. ### Delta sync, not full sync ```javascript // Never "give me all messages". Ask for what changed. GET /sync?since=historyId_8f3a → { changes: [ { type: 'message.added', message }, { type: 'message.labelsChanged', id, labels }, { type: 'message.deleted', id }, ], historyId: 'historyId_8f41', } ``` Store the `historyId` locally. On open, apply the delta and you are current in one small request. If the server says the cursor is too old (you have been away a month), fall back to a bounded resync of recent messages rather than everything. ## D — Data model ```javascript { // Normalised — a message appears in the thread, in search, in a label view. messages: { m1: { id, threadId, from, to, subject, snippet, bodyRef, receivedAt, flags } }, threads: { t1: { id, messageIds, subject, participantIds, lastMessageAt, unreadCount } }, labels: { inbox: { id, name, unreadCount } }, // Message list views are id lists, not copies. views: { inbox: { ids: [...], cursor, status } }, outbox: ['draft-8f3a'], historyId: 'historyId_8f41', } ``` **Bodies are stored separately from headers** (`bodyRef`). Listing 50,000 threads needs the subject, sender and snippet — a few hundred bytes each. Full bodies with quoted history and attachments are megabytes. Fetch a body when the message is opened, then keep it. ## O — Optimisations ### The list Virtualize — 50,000 threads is not renderable. Rows are fixed height here, which is a gift: no measurement, exact scroll positions, trivial scroll restoration. Say that you *chose* fixed-height rows to get it. Keep the label's unread count from the **server**, not from the loaded page, for the same reason a notification badge must be. ### Optimistic everything Archive, mark read, label — all instant, all reversible: ```javascript // Bulk actions must be one request, not 200. async function archive(ids) { applyLocally(ids, { removeLabel: 'inbox' }); showUndo(() => revert(ids)); // Gmail's genuinely good idea try { await api.batchModify({ ids, removeLabels: ['inbox'] }); } catch { revert(ids); toast('Could not archive — put them back'); } } ``` An **undo toast is better than a confirm dialog** for reversible destructive actions: it does not interrupt the common case and still protects the mistake. ### Compose and send Drafts autosave to IndexedDB **and** the server, debounced. The outbox is durable, so closing the tab mid-send does not lose the message; on reopen it flushes. Each send carries an idempotency key, because a retried send that duplicates an email is visible to the recipient and embarrassing. ### Search Two tiers, and naming both is the strong answer: | Tier | Where | Good for | | --- | --- | --- | | **Local** | An index over locally-held headers | Instant results while typing, works offline, covers recent mail | | **Server** | Full-text over everything | Complete, slower, needs a connection | Show local results immediately, then merge server results in as they arrive, clearly marked. Never blank the local results while waiting. ### Security — the part unique to email Email bodies are **untrusted HTML from strangers**. This is one of the most hostile rendering problems on the web: - **Sandboxed iframe** with a restrictive `sandbox` attribute, plus server-side sanitisation. Never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` an email body. - **Block remote images by default** — they are read-receipt trackers. Offer "show images" per sender. - Strip `

learnings.title: Design a calendar / scheduling app
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Google Calendar-style. The rendering is a layout puzzle; the real difficulty is **time itself** — timezones, DST, and recurrence are where correct-looking designs quietly produce wrong meetings. ## R — Requirements **Functional:** day, week and month views; create, drag to move, resize to change duration; recurring events; multiple overlaid calendars; invitees and availability. **Non-functional:** view switches feel instant; correct across timezones and DST; a year of events without jank; fully keyboard operable. ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD R["Route: /week/2026-09-12"] --> W["Window: visible range"] W --> Q["useQuery(range)"] Q --> E["Expand recurrences
for this window only"] E --> L["Layout: overlap columns"] L --> G["Grid renderer"] R --> TZ["Timezone context"] ``` ## The three genuinely hard parts ### 1. Store instants, render in a zone ```javascript // Store: UTC instant + the zone the event was CREATED in. { start: '2026-09-12T14:00:00Z', timeZone: 'Europe/London', // needed for recurrence, not just display } ``` Why both? A weekly 9am standup in London must stay **9am London** after the clocks change — not 9am UTC, which becomes 10am local. Recurrence rules are expressed in a *local* wall-clock time; the instant is derived. Storing only UTC makes every recurring meeting drift twice a year. ```javascript // Render in the VIEWER's zone, which may differ from the event's. new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', { timeZone: viewerZone, hour: '2-digit', minute: '2-digit', }).format(new Date(event.start)); ``` Show the event's own zone when it differs from the viewer's — "3pm (your time) · 9am New York" prevents an entire class of missed meetings. ### 2. DST — the two days a year that break everything - **Spring forward:** 02:30 does not exist. An event created at that wall-clock time has no instant. Reject it, or snap it forward, but decide. - **Fall back:** 01:30 happens twice. Which one? The convention is the first occurrence; say so explicitly. - **A "1-hour" meeting across the boundary is not 60 minutes of wall clock.** Drag-resize maths that assumes `end - start` in milliseconds equals the visual height will be wrong on those days. > "I'd use Temporal where available, or date-fns-tz / Luxon otherwise — and I would not do timezone arithmetic by hand. The native `Date` is genuinely unsuitable for this." ### 3. Recurrence — expand lazily, store the rule ```javascript { rrule: 'FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,WE;UNTIL=20261231T000000Z', exdates: ['2026-10-14T09:00:00Z'], // deleted occurrences overrides: { '2026-10-21T09:00:00Z': { title: 'Extended review' } }, } ``` **Never materialise every occurrence.** "Every weekday forever" is unbounded. Store the rule; expand only the occurrences inside the visible window. Editing a recurring event is a **product** decision you must surface: this occurrence, this and future, or all? Each is a different write — an `exdate` plus a new single event, a split of the rule with an `UNTIL`, or a rule edit. ## D — Data model ```javascript { view: 'week', anchorDate: '2026-09-12', // in the URL — shareable, back-button works viewerZone: 'Europe/London', events: { e1: { id, calendarId, start, end, timeZone, rrule, exdates } }, windowIndex: Map, // derived per visible range calendars: { c1: { id, name, colour, visible: true } }, } ``` ## O — Optimisations ### Overlap layout The classic interview sub-problem: N events on one day, some overlapping. Lay them out in columns. ```javascript // Sweep by start time; group events that overlap transitively into a // "cluster"; every event in a cluster shares the width. function layout(events) { const sorted = [...events].sort((a, b) => a.start - b.start || b.end - a.end); const clusters = []; let current = [], clusterEnd = -Infinity; for (const e of sorted) { if (e.start >= clusterEnd) { if (current.length) clusters.push(current); current = []; } current.push(e); clusterEnd = Math.max(clusterEnd, e.end); } if (current.length) clusters.push(current); // Within a cluster, greedily assign each event the first free column. return clusters.flatMap(assignColumns); } ``` That is `O(n log n)` and it is the answer they are looking for. The naive version compares every pair. ### Fetching Fetch by **visible range**, and prefetch the adjacent ranges — the user's next action is almost always "next week". Cache by range key so going back is instant. ### Rendering The month view can hold hundreds of events. Virtualize the day grid; render an event chip only when its day cell is visible. Use CSS grid with time-based rows rather than absolute positioning where you can — it survives zoom and text scaling far better. ### Accessibility — a grid, honestly - The calendar is `role="grid"` with `gridcell` days; arrow keys move by day, `PageUp`/`PageDown` by month - Each cell's accessible name is the **full date plus a summary** — "12 September, 3 events" — because "12" alone is meaningless out of context - Drag to move must have a keyboard equivalent: select, then a "move to" dialog or arrow-key nudging with live-region announcements - Never encode calendar identity in colour alone ## Common mistakes - **UTC only.** Recurring events drift by an hour twice a year. - **Materialising all occurrences.** Unbounded for an infinite rule. - **Native `Date` arithmetic for timezones.** It cannot do it correctly. - **Not asking "this or all occurrences?"** on edit — data loss the user did not intend. - **Pairwise overlap detection.** Quadratic on busy days. - **Colour-only calendar identity.** - **Ignoring the nonexistent and duplicated hours** on DST days. ## Key takeaways - Store the UTC instant *and* the creating timezone — recurrence needs local wall-clock semantics. - Expand recurrence lazily for the visible window only. - DST creates a missing hour and a duplicated one; decide the behaviour explicitly. - Overlap layout is a sweep into clusters, then greedy column assignment. - Use a real temporal library; never hand-roll timezone maths. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Someone flies to Tokyo mid-week."** — The viewer zone changes; events keep their instants and re-render at new local times. Offer to show both zones. - **"Find a slot for eight people."** — Intersect free/busy on the server, not the client. Fetch availability windows, not everyone's events — that is also a privacy boundary. - **"A recurring event 'every last Friday'."** — `BYDAY=-1FR`. Use a real RRULE library; the edge cases in RFC 5545 are endless.

learnings.title: Design a live map with moving vehicles
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Uber/Lyft-style. A rendering and interpolation problem wearing a maps costume: positions arrive every few seconds, and the vehicle must appear to move continuously. ## R — Requirements **Functional:** a map with your location; nearby vehicles moving in real time; a route line and ETA; pickup pin selection; the driver's position during a trip. **Non-functional:** vehicles move **smoothly**, not in jumps; 60 fps while panning with 200 vehicles visible; works on a poor mobile connection; must not drain the battery. > "How often do positions arrive? If it's every 4 seconds, the hard part isn't the network — it's making a 4-second-old jump look like continuous motion." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD WS["Position stream
(SSE, one update / 4s)"] --> B["Viewport filter"] B --> I["Interpolation buffer
previous + target per vehicle"] I --> RAF["requestAnimationFrame"] RAF --> L["WebGL marker layer"] M["Map tiles"] --> L ``` ### Interpolation is the whole trick A position every 4 seconds rendered directly means a car that teleports four times a minute. Instead, hold the previous and target positions and animate between them: ```javascript // Each frame, move every vehicle a fraction of the way to its target. function frame(now) { for (const v of vehicles.values()) { const t = Math.min(1, (now - v.updatedAt) / UPDATE_INTERVAL); v.lat = lerp(v.prevLat, v.targetLat, t); v.lng = lerp(v.prevLng, v.targetLng, t); v.bearing = lerpAngle(v.prevBearing, v.targetBearing, t); // shortest arc } layer.setData(vehicles); requestAnimationFrame(frame); } ``` Two details that separate a good answer: - **Interpolate the bearing along the shortest arc.** Going from 350° to 10° must rotate 20° forward, not 340° backward. A car spinning on its axis is the classic bug. - **You are always rendering the past.** Interpolating *toward* a known position means displaying a vehicle up to one interval behind reality. Extrapolating ahead looks smoother and is sometimes wrong — it will overshoot when the car stops at a light. Interpolation is the safer default; say you considered both. **Snap to roads** server-side. A raw GPS trace wanders off the road; map-matched positions look correct and cost the client nothing. ## D — Data model ```javascript { viewport: { center, zoom, bounds }, vehicles: Map, trip: { driverId, route: encodedPolyline, etaSeconds } | null, } ``` ## O — Optimisations ### Render markers on the GPU 200 DOM markers, each repositioned every frame, is 200 style recalculations per frame. It will not hold 60 fps. Use the map library's **WebGL layer** (Mapbox GL `symbol` layer, deck.gl `ScatterplotLayer`). One draw call for all markers; position updates are a buffer write, not a DOM mutation. Keep the DOM for the *chrome* — bottom sheet, buttons, the ETA card. ### Subscribe to the viewport Only stream vehicles inside the current bounds plus a margin. On pan, update the subscription — debounced, so a drag does not fire twenty subscription changes. At low zoom, **cluster** rather than drawing every vehicle: nobody can distinguish 400 cars at city zoom, and the server should not send them. ### Battery and data This runs on a phone, often in a car: - Pause the stream and the animation loop when the tab is hidden (`visibilitychange`) - Lower the update rate when the user is not actively looking at the map - `navigator.geolocation.watchPosition` with a sensible `maximumAge`; high-accuracy GPS continuously is a battery killer - Respect `saveData` ### Route and ETA The route is an **encoded polyline** — a compact string, not an array of thousands of coordinates. Decode client-side and render as a line layer. The ETA comes from the server (it knows traffic) but should tick down smoothly on the client between updates rather than jumping. ### Accessibility — a map is not usable by everyone A canvas map is opaque to a screen reader. The credible answer is a **parallel non-visual interface**: - A text summary that updates politely: "Driver is 3 minutes away, approaching on Mill Road" - A list view of nearby vehicles with distance and direction as an alternative to the map - Full keyboard operation for the actual task — choosing a pickup point must not require dragging a pin. Offer address entry and a list of nearby named places. > "The task is 'get picked up', not 'use a map'. I'd make sure the whole task can be completed without the map at all — that's better for screen reader users and also for anyone on a bad connection." ## Common mistakes - **Rendering raw positions.** Vehicles teleport. - **Naive bearing interpolation.** Cars spin when crossing 0°. - **DOM markers at scale.** Cannot hold frame rate. - **Streaming everything regardless of viewport.** - **Running the animation loop in a hidden tab.** - **Continuous high-accuracy geolocation.** Drains the battery. - **No non-map path through the task.** ## Key takeaways - Interpolate between the previous and target positions every frame; that is what makes motion smooth. - Interpolate bearing along the shortest arc, and prefer interpolation over extrapolation. - WebGL layers for markers, DOM for chrome. - Subscribe to the viewport and cluster at low zoom. - Provide a complete non-map path through the task. ## Interview follow-ups - **"The connection drops for 30 seconds."** — Stop animating after one interval rather than drifting on stale data, show the position as stale, and snap to the true position on reconnect rather than animating a huge jump. - **"10,000 vehicles in the city?"** — The server clusters and sends aggregates by zoom; the client never sees 10,000. - **"Why not extrapolate?"** — It looks smoother until the car stops and the marker sails through the junction. Interpolation is a fixed, honest lag; extrapolation is a variable, dishonest one.

learnings.title: Design an order-tracking experience
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Food delivery, parcel tracking, support tickets. A smaller question that tests something specific: can you model a **state machine** properly, and do you handle the states that go backwards?

## R — Requirements

**Functional:** a progress timeline of order stages; live courier location once out for delivery; ETA; push and in-app notifications on stage change; order history.
**Non-functional:** the page is opened repeatedly and briefly, so it must load fast; correct even if the user leaves it open for an hour; works when the tab is backgrounded.

## A — Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Order page"] --> Q["useQuery(order)"]
  Q --> SSE["SSE — order.updated"]
  SSE --> Q
  P --> M["Map — only while out for delivery"]
  P --> N["Push — via service worker"]
```

**SSE, not WebSocket.** Updates flow server→client only; the client never sends anything on this stream. Choosing SSE here and being able to say why is a cheap, reliable signal.

## D — Model the states explicitly

```javascript
const STAGES = ['placed', 'confirmed', 'preparing', 'out_for_delivery', 'delivered'];

{
  orderId,
  stage: 'preparing',
  stageHistory: [{ stage: 'placed', at }, { stage: 'confirmed', at }],
  eta: { earliest, latest, confidence: 'high' | 'low' },
  courier: { id, name, lat, lng } | null,     // only when out_for_delivery
  exception: null | { type: 'delayed' | 'cancelled' | 'failed_delivery', message },
}
```

### The states everyone forgets

A happy-path timeline of five stages is the easy version. The question is really about the rest:

| State | Why it breaks a naive design |
| --- | --- |
| **Cancelled** | The timeline must stop and explain, not sit at step 2 forever |
| **Delayed** | The ETA moved backwards. Say so explicitly — a silently changing ETA destroys trust |
| **Failed delivery** | A terminal state that is not "delivered" and needs an action |
| **Returned to store** | The progress bar goes *backwards* |
| **Partially fulfilled** | One order, two shipments, two timelines |

> "I'd model this as an explicit state machine with the exception states as first-class, not as a linear progress bar with a percentage. The moment an order can go backwards, a progress bar is lying."

### ETA honesty

An ETA that quietly slides from 20 minutes to 45 is the most-complained-about behaviour in every delivery product. Two rules:

- **Show a range, not a point** — "20–30 min" is honest; "23 min" implies precision nobody has
- **When it moves significantly, say so.** "Running about 10 minutes late — the kitchen is busy" is far better received than a number that quietly grew

## O — Optimisations

### Load the sensible amount

The order page is opened many times for a few seconds each. Server-render the current stage so it is readable instantly, and **only then** connect the stream. Do not make someone wait on a WebSocket handshake to learn their food is being cooked.

The map is the expensive part — a map library is hundreds of kilobytes. **Load it lazily, and only when the stage is `out_for_delivery`.** Most views of this page never reach that stage.

### Background behaviour

The tab will be backgrounded for most of the order's life:

- Close the stream on `visibilitychange` and refetch on return; an hour-long idle SSE connection per user is real server cost
- Use **push notifications** for stage changes, not a permanently open connection
- On return, refetch rather than trusting an hour-old cached stage

### Notifications

Notify on stage change, deduplicated with the in-app path so a user with the tab open does not get both a toast and an OS notification. Ask for push permission **after the order is placed** — that is the moment the user has obvious reason to say yes.

### Accessibility

- The timeline is an ordered list with a clear current step, not just a styled row of dots
- Stage changes are announced in a **polite** live region — "Your order is out for delivery"
- Never encode stage by colour alone; each step needs a text label
- The ETA has a text form; an animated progress bar alone communicates nothing
- If the map is present, the courier's position also needs a text form: "3 minutes away, on Mill Road"

## Common mistakes

- **A linear percentage bar.** Cannot express cancelled, failed, or returned.
- **Exception states bolted on late.** They are the states that matter most to the user.
- **ETA as a precise number that silently changes.**
- **Loading the map library up front.** Most sessions never need it.
- **Holding an SSE connection open in a hidden tab for an hour.**
- **Stage conveyed by colour alone.**

## Key takeaways

- Model it as a state machine with exceptions as first-class states, not a progress percentage.
- Server-render the current stage; connect the stream afterwards.
- Lazy-load the map, and only when the order is actually out for delivery.
- Close the stream when hidden and rely on push for the long tail.
- Show ETA as a range and announce meaningful changes out loud.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"The order is cancelled while they are watching."** — The stream pushes the exception; the timeline switches to a terminal cancelled state with the reason and the refund status. Never leave the old timeline visible.
- **"They open it on two devices."** — Both subscribe; state is server-owned so they agree. Push must be deduplicated per user, not per device.
- **"How would you test it?"** — Drive the state machine directly in tests, including every backwards and terminal transition. The happy path is the least interesting case.

learnings.title: Design a booking flow with seat selection
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Flights, cinemas, events. The defining constraint is **contention**: many people want the same seat at the same time, and the UI has to be honest about the fact that seeing a seat does not mean having it. ## R — Requirements **Functional:** a seat map with availability and pricing tiers; select one or more seats; a hold while you pay; payment; confirmation with tickets. **Non-functional:** availability is fresh enough to be believable; **a seat is never sold twice**; the hold expires visibly; the seat map is usable without a mouse or sight. > "How much contention? A cinema on a Tuesday and a stadium the minute tickets drop are the same UI and completely different systems — one needs a queue in front of it." ## A — Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Seat map"] --> A["GET /availability
(snapshot)"] S --> SSE["SSE — seat.taken / seat.released"] S --> H["POST /holds
→ holdId + expiresAt"] H --> T["Countdown timer"] T --> P["Payment"] P --> O["POST /orders (idempotent)"] T -->|expired| R["Release + tell the user"] ``` ## The hold is the centre of the design Selecting a seat must **reserve it server-side immediately**, before payment: ```javascript async function selectSeat(seatId) { markPending(seatId); // optimistic, visibly provisional try { const hold = await api.createHold({ seatIds: [...selected, seatId] }); setHold(hold); // { holdId, expiresAt } } catch (err) { if (err.code === 'SEAT_TAKEN') { markTaken(seatId); toast('Someone just took that seat'); // say what happened } unmarkPending(seatId); } } ``` Without a hold, two people pay for the same seat and one of them gets an apology email. **The hold is what makes the flow correct**, and the server enforces it — a client-side "selected" state is decoration. ### The countdown must be visible and honest ```javascript // Drive from the server's expiresAt, never from a local countdown that // started when the component mounted. Client clocks drift, tabs freeze. const remaining = Math.max(0, expiresAt - serverNow()); ``` - Show the timer prominently — "Your seats are held for 7:42" - Warn before expiry, and offer to extend if the business allows it - On expiry, **release and say so clearly**. Silently losing the seats mid-payment is the worst possible version of this flow. - Compute from the server's `expiresAt`, because a backgrounded mobile tab has its timers throttled and a locally-counted timer will be wrong ## D — Data model ```javascript { eventId, seats: Map, hold: { holdId, seatIds, expiresAt } | null, selection: Set, } ``` `pending` is separate from `held_by_me` — it is the optimistic state between click and server confirmation, and it must look provisional so a rejection is not a surprise. ## O — Optimisations ### Rendering a large seat map A stadium is 50,000 seats. As DOM elements it is unusable. - **SVG** works to a few thousand seats and gives you hit-testing, focus and ARIA for free - Beyond that, **canvas** with a spatial index for hit-testing, plus a zoomed-in DOM overlay for the section the user is actually looking at - Almost always the right answer is **section first, then seats**: pick a section from a small overview, then render only that section's seats. It matches how people choose anyway, and it removes the scaling problem entirely. ### Keeping availability believable Full availability for 50,000 seats is a large payload and stale immediately. - Fetch a snapshot **for the visible section only** - Subscribe to SSE deltas for that section; unsubscribe on navigating away - Refetch on tab focus — someone gone for five minutes has a stale map - Accept that it will be slightly stale, and **design for the rejection** rather than pretending it will not happen ### High contention — the queue For a sale with severe contention, a waiting room in front of the flow is the honest design: a queue token, a position, and an estimated wait. It converts a site that falls over into a site that is slow but working, and users tolerate a visible queue far better than a spinner that fails. ### Accessibility — where seat maps usually fail completely A seat map is the classic "beautiful and unusable" component. - Every seat is a **real focusable control** with an accessible name that carries the whole context: "Row F, seat 12, premium, £85, available" - Arrow keys move within the grid; the map is `role="grid"` with rows - **Provide a non-map alternative**: "best available for 3 people together" is faster for nearly everyone and is the only usable path for some - Never encode availability by colour alone — use shape or a text/pattern distinction - Announce selection changes and the running total in a polite live region > "I'd make sure the whole purchase can be completed without ever using the visual map. 'Two seats together, cheapest' is genuinely the better interface for most people, and it happens to be the accessible one." ## Common mistakes - **Selecting without holding.** Two people pay for one seat. - **A client-side countdown.** Wrong after a backgrounded tab. - **Silent expiry.** The seats vanish mid-payment with no explanation. - **Fetching the whole venue's availability.** - **A seat map with no non-visual alternative.** - **Colour-only availability.** - **No idempotency key on the final order.** ## Key takeaways - The hold is the design: reserve server-side on selection, before payment. - Drive the countdown from the server's `expiresAt`, and make expiry loud. - Section first, then seats — it solves the rendering problem and matches user behaviour. - Snapshot plus SSE deltas for the visible section; refetch on focus. - "Best available" is the faster path for most users and the accessible one. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Two people select the same seat at the same instant."** — The server grants one hold; the loser gets `SEAT_TAKEN`, sees the seat flip to taken, and is told why. The optimistic `pending` state is what makes that recoverable rather than jarring. - **"The hold expires during payment."** — Do not silently fail the charge. Check the hold before submitting, and if it has gone, stop and explain before taking money. - **"100,000 people at 9am."** — A waiting room. The seat map is not the bottleneck; the hold endpoint is.
